title: Judah's plea (Genesis 44:18–34)
hookLine: Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place

lines: THE ONE WITH THE CUP STAYS.
THE BROTHER WHO SAID SELL HIM.
cards: The room is silent. The governor of Egypt has just said: the one with the cup stays as my slave; the rest of you, go. The brothers are on the floor.
Benjamin stands there, the cup found in his bag, his whole life about to be taken away. And the Torah says: "Then Judah came near unto him." In Hebrew it's one word, vayigash: and he drew near.
Nobody tells him to. Nobody expects him to. Judah, who years ago looked at another brother in a pit and said, let's sell him, walks up to the man who holds all their lives.

teach.b: Judah's speech isn't clever. It's a story.
He tells the governor about their old father, and the son of his old age, whose brother is dead, the only one left from his mother, whom his father loves.
He quotes his father's own words: you know my wife bore me two sons; one went out from me, and I said, surely he is torn in pieces, and I haven't seen him since.

If you take this one too, and harm comes to him, you'll bring my gray hairs down with sorrow to the grave. Listen to what Judah is doing. He's saying out loud that their father has a favorite, and accepting it.
The old jealousy is nowhere to be heard. He tells how he made himself surety for the boy, promising to bring him home.

teach.h: LET ME STAY INSTEAD OF THE LAD.
teach.b: Then the offer: "let thy servant, I pray thee, abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren." Take me instead. I'll be your slave for the rest of my life.
And the last line: "For how shall I go up to my father, if the lad be not with me?" Think about who's hearing this.

teach.h: HOW SHALL I GO UP TO MY FATHER?
teach.b: The brother who was sold into slavery listens as the brother who said sell him offers to become a slave, so that a brother, and a father, won't suffer what Joseph and Jacob suffered.
First with Tamar, and now here, Judah is the brother who owns what he did, and then does better.

how: Judah's plea opens the weekly Torah portion Vayigash, read in synagogue each winter, and rabbinic teaching remembers Judah as a man who owned his wrongs.

o: Judah offers himself as a slave so Benjamin can go
Judah argues that Benjamin never took the cup
Judah begs for mercy for the whole family

games.q: what's inside the plea — tap the pairs.
p: Judah's promise to bring the boy home

s: Judah argued that Benjamin was innocent
he didn't argue about the cup. he told the story of their father and offered himself instead.
Judah quotes his own father's words to the governor
my wife bore me two sons; one went out from me, and I said, surely he is torn in pieces.
Judah was the brother who suggested selling Joseph
in Genesis 37 he said, let's sell him. here he offers himself as a slave.

games.q: you're Judah. you promised your father you'd bring Benjamin home. now the governor says Benjamin stays as a slave. what do you do?
o: go home and tell your father the truth.
offer to stay as a slave in his place.
try to steal Benjamin back at night.
games.why: he draws near and offers himself: let me stay instead of the lad. it's the speech that breaks Joseph open.

practice: Think of someone near you who's carrying too much right now: a parent with a sick kid, a friend in a hard month, a coworker buried in work.
Find one concrete thing you could take off their hands, a meal, a ride, a shift, an afternoon of childcare, not a vague let me know. Decide who, and what.

wordCard.voice: Judah's plea. The brother who once said sell him draws near and offers himself as a slave, so that Benjamin can go home.

orig.note: Hebrew: and he drew near. the first word of Judah's plea, and the name of the Torah portion.

carryVoice: Your line: take me instead. A pledge kept, at his own cost. That's day seventy-three.
